魏王 is the title Prince of Wei and 繼岌 is Li Jiji's personal name; the proposed order is correct.

In Tang, Prince Ji Ji of Wei was Director of the Xingsheng Palace and concurrently held the post of military commissioner of Zhen Prefecture; the legal officer Li Rao was put in charge of secretarial records.

In Tang, Li Jiji, Prince of Wei, was Director of the Xingsheng Palace and concurrently held the post of military commissioner of Zhen Prefecture; the legal officer Li Rao was put in charge of secretarial records.
The literal field repeats the same title-name inversion and should identify Li Jiji clearly.

鹽鐵判官 is a subordinate administrative judge or assistant, not the salt-and-iron commissioner.

The literal translation must likewise distinguish 判官 from the commissioner who headed the office.

In the Changxing era, Emperor Mingzong was advanced in years; Prince Qin Li Congrong was often lawless; Jin Gaozu was deputy commander of the Six Armies, feared calamity would reach him, and sought appointment outside the capital as a frontier commissioner.
晉高祖 is the conventional temple name Jin Gaozu, not a phrase meaning 'the Jin high ancestor.'

丁內艱 specifically means entering mourning for one's mother.

He entered mourning for his mother and was recalled before mourning was ended.
The literal field should preserve the explicit maternal mourning indicated by 內艱.
Later, when the Khitan prince Ma withdrew from Zhenzhou, Song returned with Feng Dao and the others.
Later, when the Khitan general Mada abandoned Zhenzhou, Song returned with Feng Dao and the others.

The chapter's 麻 is a truncated reference to the Khitan general Mada (麻荅), identified in parallel passages. Removing the invented princely title is right, but the full attested name should be restored.
